The meeting, which was intended to quell resident concerns over recent changes in land use laws and plans by a developer to build two large homes plus an ADU in a heavily wooded area with a creek on Wistaria Way. The meeting, led by Planning Director Kevin Jackson, seemed to only further expose the divisions between City Hall and community members, notably the 30 or so who attended. The meeting which the City named the “Housing Accountability Act Primer,” consisted of a presentation on the specifics of new state laws SB9, SB35, and the Housing Accountability Act followed by a Q&A session with city officials. This communal prayer originated with the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of its temple in 586 BCE. articles.text: Why should City rely solely on developer for all information? Editor: The following letter was sent on July 30 to members of Piedmont City Council. The recent dispute over the City’s grant of a lot-split and multiple-family development at 77 Wistaria way exposed several flaws in the City’s execution of the new state housing mandate known as “SB 9.” True, SB 9 places real constraints on local government zoning and land-use regulation. The City Council, however, has gratuitously embraced those constraints – and others – in an attempt to attract new housing that will increase the City’s tax base, subsidized school headcounts and the overly optimistic housing element plan. With nary a vote of the residents, Piedmont has opened a secretive fast-track highway to any developer who wants to tum a quick profit by building four dwellings on a property meant for one or two. The City Council added Division 17.54 to the City Code to administer the new constraints imposed by SB 9. But in its haste to embrace the new law, I believe the City Council has run roughshod over three core fairness principles that should govern its service on behalf of the citizens and voters of Piedmont: (1) Public transparency, notice and an opportunity to be heard, (2) administrative reasonableness and accountability and (3) the balancing of developers’ rights with the rights of our residents to avoid adverse impacts on their health, safety and environment. Why should a decision so consequential to our community take place in secret, without accountability? And why should the City rely solely on the developer for all of the information relevant to its decision? The recent Wistaria Way dispute has shown that Division 17.54 needs to be revised immediately in order to satisfy these three fairness principles. Accordingly, I respectfully request that the City Council amend Division 17.54 of the City Code to include the following elements, all of which are compliant with SB 9: 1. Upon receipt of an application under SB 9, the Director shall promptly notify nearby residents of the subject property. The notice shall include (a) a description of the application and proposed development, (b) the likely timetable for the City’s consideration/action, and (c) an invitation to provide facts relating to the qualification for SB 9 treatment and whether there would be any specific, adverse impact on health, safety or the environment by the proposed development. The notice shall also be published in the next edition of the Piedmont Post newspaper. 2. The Director shall consider all material received in connection with the application before rendering a decision on the application, as required by Code section 17.54.040.E. 3. The Director’s written decision under Code section 17.54.040 E. shall specifically address the “specific, adverse impacts” language of SB 9 and make specific findings thereon. The Director’s findings shall be based upon reasonable inquiry. 4. The Director may not delegate his/her responsibilities under section 17.54.040 to subordinate staff, although staff may provide support and resources to assist the Director’s determinations. 5. The Director shall promptly notify nearby residents of the approval or denial of the application following issuance of his/her written decision. The notice shall also be published in the next edition of the Piedmont Post newspaper. 6. The Director shall promptly notify nearby residents of any further permit applications being submitted following the approval of the SB 9 application. The notice(s) shall also be published in the next edition of the Piedmont Post newspaper. 7 The City Council reserves the right to review the Director’s decision on the application for compliance with administrative mandamus law, pursuant to City Charter section 2.09. (Ministerial administrative acts like those required by SB 9 still must pass the test that they are “neither arbitrary, capricious nor without reasonable evidentiary support.” When legitimate questions arise, the City Council must reserve its Charter authority under Sec. 2.09 to assure that the Director’s ministerial approval of an SB 9 application passes this test. 8 Current provisions of Division 17.54 that conflict with these provisions shall be amended to be consistent with these provisions. The citizens and voters of Piedmont deserve your endorsement of fundamental fairness, and your direction to City administrative staff to treat us with respect and due concern for our well-being. We will wait and see if you are willing to demonstrate your devotion to these core principles. Respectfully, –Harvey L. Leidmerman Piedmont resident Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Nearly half (46%) of Piedmont’s greenhouse gas emissions come from passenger vehicles according to the most recent Piedmont Greenhouse Gas Inventory, which Sustainability Division staff presented to City Council on July 1. The report, based on 2022, showed that local emissions have been stagnant or increasing in recent years. Meeting the City’s goal of carbon neutrality by 2045 will require significant changes in the way we live, work, and move – including greater adoption of electric vehicles (EVs). Though a 2021 survey found that 74% of Piedmonters without an EV had considered purchasing or leasing one, respondents reported that concerns about lack of charging stations, insufficient driving range, and purchase price were holding them back from making the switch. Models do offer varying battery capacities, but calculating your daily commute, typical weekend mileage, and extended trip mileage can help you find those that fit your needs. Coupled with the many benefits of EVs, such as reduced tailpipe emissions and at-home “fueling” for homeowners, market evolution is making EVs an increasingly attractive transportation mode. In the next year dozens of new models are set to debut. A few cars even allow special “bidirectional charging,” which turns your car into a battery that can power your home during outages. If you’re ready to make the switch, visit driveclean.ca.gov to start browsing models and exploring incentives. articles.text: Meet Neptune, a lively and treat-loving pup with a personality as big as his wagging tail. Neptune is four-years-old and weighs 80 pounds. Shelter staff report he already knows how to sit and shake and that he has strong recall off leash. articles.text: Residents interested in running for City Council or Piedmont School Board can pick up nomination documents from the City Clerk. The deadline for all applicants is this Friday, August 9. On November 5, Piedmont voters will elect candidates to fill two City Council seats and three Board of Education seats. Councilmember Conna McCarthy and Board of Education members Hilary Cooper and Veronica Anderson Thigpen are eligible for re-election. Mayor Jen Cavenaugh and Board of Education member Cory Smegal will be termed out. The nomination process can be complicated, and filing deadlines are tight, so interested residents should begin as soon as possible. If you are interested in running: 1. Make an appointment with the City Clerk’s office at 420- 3040 or CityClerk@piedmont. ca.gov to obtain your candidate documents. At your appointment, the City Clerk will walk you through the nomination process, reviewing the different documents, deadlines and rules involved. Plan on spending 30-60 minutes. 2. Review the fundamentals of the process online. Prepare for your appointment by reading about running for office on the City website. This will give you an idea of what to expect and allow you to identify questions you may want to ask during your appointment. 3. Submit your nomination documents by Friday, August 9. Nomination documents must be filed in person at the City Clerk’s office. It is a good idea for candidates to file documents early so they can correct any errors that come up. I can’t believe my city is doing this.” – David Ashton, a third-generation Piedmont resident Staff Photos City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore prepares to read questions from the audience. staff members – including City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, Jackson, Building Official Paki Muthig, Fire Captain Mike Carlisle and Manager Echa Schneider – sat at the front of the room prepared to take questions from residents via written cards. “These are big changes and shifts in how the city is carrying out work as it relates to housing production in the city of Piedmont,” said Bayon Moore. The California Housing Opportunity and More Efficiency (HOME) Act also known as “SB9” (Senate Bill 9) continues to be a controversial subject in Piedmont. The law, effective January 1, 2022, allows homeowners to create up to four homes on an existing parcel. As UC Berkeley’s Terner Center for Housing Innovation notes, this state law effectively eliminates single-family-only zoning. The law allows the owner to “split” its lot, which makes it easier to sell or finance additional homes on a single parcel. While proponents believe the law will help address the current housing crisis in California by opening new opportunities for small-scale homebuilding, critics of SB9 are concerned the law may lead to speculation and unchecked growth at the expense of a community’s character and traditions. Bayon Moore made it clear at the beginning of the night that officials would not be taking questions on specific projects and that the night was for general housing law questions only – a reference to the attention the City has received in recent weeks for allowing a controversial construction project on Wistaria Way, which was approved via an SB9 application and with little public input. The greatest point of contention between city officials and residents appears to be over how much the city government is allowed to do and its lack of transparency during this process. Throughout its presentation, the city argued that its hands are tied by limitations in SB9. “Cities must facilitate housing, and the state is requiring us to do that by adjusting local regulations consistent with state law, streamlining the process to process permits for housing development, and developing checklists and information for potential developers,” said Jackson. Jackson also laid out his understanding of the penalties for Piedmont at the state level for not complying with SB9, including the withholding of state funding and potential lawsuits from applicants and the Attorney General’s office. However, many residents remain outraged and believe City Hall should be doing more to defend the interests of its citizens and the character of its neighborhoods. “I don’t feel like City Council and staff appreciate that SB9 lot splits are not a desired outcome to the current residents and citizens,” said Rich Latvala, who lives near the city’s first SB9-approved project at 77 Wistaria Way. Many residents also believe that SB9, as it is currently being enforced, lacks refinement. One example they have cited is the city’s policy regarding moveins. SB9 is intended for use by homeowners, not institutional investors. As such, developers must sign an affidavit confirming they will live in the home they are building for at least three years. City officials admit there is no way of enforcing this, potentially opening neighborhoods to unchecked development. “When I bought my home, I had the guarantee of a single-family-zoned lot. I never anticipated high-density housing in my backyard. And now, that’s what I’m getting,” said David Ashton, a lifetime Piedmont resident who lives near Wistaria Way. Tensions were palpable during the one-hour meeting. “[The meeting] attempted to answer some questions, but basically presented even more questions about the implementation of SB9,” said Latvala. “I have lost faith in my local government. I can’t believe my city is doing this,” exclaimed Ashton, a third-generation resident. Bayon Moore urged concerned residents to contact their state representatives, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks and Senator Nancy Skinner, about “areas of concern” or “the changes that have taken place.” The meeting was attended by more than 30 people, who filed in gradually as the meeting got underway. articles.text: and Ariel Rodriguez The school year is starting again, and this time of transition can feel both exciting and overwhelming. As we enter the new school year we have the unique opportunity to make a fresh start: new classes, new teachers, and, perhaps, a new perspective. Here are some steps to help you start the school year feeling empowered. Step 1 - Reflect For many of us, the start of the school year can feel like a mad scramble. Setting aside even a few minutes to reflect on the previous school year can make a meaningful difference. Ask yourself, “What worked well last school year and how did that make me feel?” Then, ask yourself, “What was challenging last school year and how did that make me feel?” Write down a few responses for each question. Keep your responses brief, but try to be specific. Here are some examples: – “having a separate binder for each class helped me feel organized” – “we usually run late on Monday mornings which makes me feel anxious” Step 2 - Plan If something is working for you, don’t change it! Acknowledge how helpful it’s been and re-commit to that behavior going forward. Once you identify a challenge, acknowledge that it exists and work to make changes. If Monday mornings feel frantic and stressful in your household, write down some ideas for how you might be able to change that: – “pick out Monday’s outfit on Sunday” – “pack my backpack on Sunday evening” After you’ve made your list of ideas, pick one or two to try. Step 3 - Check in For the last month, you’ve used Sunday to pick Monday’s outfit and to pack your backpack. Do you feel less stressed? Are you making it to school on time? If the answer is yes - congratulations! You’ve found a behavior that helps you overcome a challenge. Keep doing what you’re doing. If the answer is no, that’s ok. Go back to your list and try another idea from your brainstorm until you find something that does work for you. This process of checking in with yourself is especially helpful during times of transition and can help you feel empowered to grow not only as a student but as a person! articles.text: Tennis Town, California appears to have another pupil on the rise. Isaac Milner, a fifth grader at Havens Elementary, brought home a trophy after winning the Little Mo West Regional Tennis Tournament at the Berkeley Tennis Club on July 22. The tournament is named after tennis great Maureen Connolly who died at age 35. The “Little Mo” began in 1976 in Dallas and expanded to a nationwide competition in 1998. It is considered one of the premier series of junior tournaments for girls and boys tennis stars. It is the only circuit of its kind for high-performance girls and boys in the United States. Competing in a field of 32 athletes, Milner squared off with Daniel Mac Sy of Rocklin in the Final. Milner dropped the first set 6-3, but powered back in the second set to claim a 6-4 victory and force a 10-point tiebreaker, which he won 10-6. “My instant reaction to winning was pure happiness because I won the whole thing!” Milner said ecstatically. Milner had some trouble finding his form in the first set, allowing Sy to claim the first set. But Milner altered his strategy to get on the offensive, slamming forehand and backhand winners to tie things up. In the tiebreaker, Milner got out to an early 5-1 lead and kept his foot on the gas pedal toward the victory. “In the final, I lost the first set because I was making more errors than normal. In the second set, I played better and more offensively. In the final tiebreaker I jumped to a 5-1 lead, then I tried to stay on offense and was able to win,” he said To get there, Milner had shutout victories in the Round of 32 and Round of 16 with a pair of dominant 6-0, 6-0 wins. In the Quarterfinals he continued his high execuIsaac Milner, 10, stands proudly with his first-place trophy after winning the Little Mo West Regional Tennis Tournament. tion with a 6-2, 6-0 win, following up with another dominant 6-3, 6-0 win in the semifinals. Milner is coached twice a week with Piedmont High tennis coach Jim Landes. Landes praised Isaac for his tenacity on the court, showing rare skill for someone his age. “What struck me when I first met Isaac was his drive and focus. When he practices, he concentrates from the first ball to the last—he ever wastes a moment. He runs for every ball and knows just what he wants to do with it, that’s very rare for someone his age. He is also very talented with great speed, timing and coordination,” Landes said. Milner has qualified for and will compete in the Little Mo Nationals in Austin, Texas on September 27-30. Isaac Milner (right) squared off with Daniel Mac Sy of Rocklin, winning in three sets. Milner will now compete in the Little Mo Nationals in Austin, Texas in September.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Spectrum News Katie Ledecky made history by winning her ninth Olympic gold medal, the most decorated women’s Olympics swimmer of all time. The 2024 Summer Olympics are underway in Paris, France and continue through August 11. As of August 6, the United States holds first place in the medal count with 23 golds, 31 silvers and 29 bronze medals. Host country France has the third most medals with 13 golds, 16 silvers, and 18 bronze medals through Day 12. Here’s a rundown of some of the best moments from this year’s Olympic Games. Katie Ledecky makes history U.S. swimmer Katie Ledecky made the history books as the most successful women’s swimmer to ever compete in the Olympics. Ledecky’s victory in the 800 meter freestyle with a time of 8:11.04 on August 3, marked the ninth gold medal of her career to overtake Jenny Thompson’s record set in 2004. It also marked Ledecky’s second gold medal at this year’s Olympic Games after winning the 1500 meter freestyle on July 31 with an Olympic record time of 15:30.02. Team USA Men’s Gymnastics wins first medal since 1998 On July 29, Team USA’s men’s gymnastics team won its first medal in 16 years after Brody Malone, Frederick Richard, Asher Hong, Paul Juda, and Stephen Nedoroscik took bronze (3rd place) in the artistic team allaround event. Nedoroscik had one of the most wholesome moments in an interview reflecting on the moments before dismounting from the pommel horse while re-watching his routine, knowing he just needed to get his job done to make history for the U.S. “Going up to pommel horse, I’m the last guy in the whole competition. I had a good feeling that our team was in a great spot, I just knew I had to go up there and do my job. I was super worried in my routine, I was thinking, ‘Let’s just get it done! Let’s go for it!’ Right here, I was like, ‘If I put this dismount up, Team USA gets a medal!’ You can see it right away when I land, I’m getting goosebumps right now, this is the best moment of my life,” Nedoroscik said. Noah Lyles wins Team USA’s first 100 meter since 2004 On August 4, Noah Lyles won the 100 meter dash with a time of 9.79 seconds to earn gold and tying the 12th fastest time in history set by American Maurice Green in 1999. Lyles becomes the first U.S. 100 meter sprinter to win Olympic gold since Justin Gatlin in 2004 in Athens, Greece. Simone Biles also makes history Simone Biles is back on top as the most decorated Olympic Gymnast to ever compete. She has secured three gold medals and one silver, her 11th medal and seventh gold. On July 30, she helped lead the U.S. to gold in the artistic team all-around event then put a stamp on the record by winning gold in women’s gymnastics all-around on August 1. Two days later, Biles also won the vault, and on August 5 she took silver in the women’s floor event. Sha’Carri Richardson wins first medal It may not have gone the way she envisioned, but track sprinter Sha’Carri Richardson claimed the first Olympic medal of her racing career after placing second in the 100 meter dash on August 3. After a slow start out of the blocks, Richardson stormed back to second place. But the event’s winner, Julien Alfred, made history for her country of St. Lucia, winning gold and becoming the only athlete to ever win a medal for the small East Caribbean island nation of just 180,857 people. articles.text: The Monk’s Trail to Wat Pha Lat & Wat Phra That Doi Suthep [Reprinted from August 2023 Piedmont Post.] In our first international hiking story, we discover the wonders of Thailand. Welcome travelers, hikers, and traveling hikers. Thailand is home to some of the thickest jungles in the world. Luckily, the outskirts of Chiang Mai provides a scenic hike through a Thai jungle on its way to a pair of historic Buddhist temples. The Monk’s Trail, also known as the Wat Pha Lat Trail, takes hikers to a hidden temple, Wat Pha Lat, within the Doi Suthep-Pui National Park. The hike to Wat Pha Lat is just 0.8 of a mile but ascends a steep 550 feet in elevation gain. During the hike to Wat Pha Lat, you’ll pass under groves of bamboo with insects making noise around you, while also passing a small waterfall on your way to the temple. Wat Pha Lat translates to “Monastery at the Sloping Rock.” Created during the reign of King Kuena from 1355-1385, the monastery was originally used as a resting spot for people walking up to at Phra That Doi Suthep, the much famous and final location for our hike. Once the road leading to Doi Suthep was established in 1935, Wat Pha Lat became a residency for monks. You’re welcomed to the holy grounds by sculptures of Buddha with a cascading stream of water falling over the sloping Statues of Buddha greet you as you enter Wat Pha Lat. Welcome travelers, hikers, and traveling hikers. Thailand is home to some of the thickest jungles in the world. Luckily, the outskirts of Chiang Mai provides a scenic hike through a Thai jungle on its way to a pair of historic Buddhist temples. The Monk’s Trail, also known as the Wat Pha Lat Trail, takes hikers to a hidden temple, Wat Pha Lat, within the Doi Suthep-Pui National Park. The hike to Wat Pha Lat is just 0.8 of a mile but ascends a steep 550 feet in elevation gain. During the hike to Wat Pha Lat, you’ll pass under groves of bamboo with insects making noise around you, while also passing a small waterfall on your way to the temple. Wat Pha Lat translates to “Monastery at the Sloping Rock.” Created during the reign of King Kuena from 1355-1385, the monastery was originally used as a resting spot for people walking up to at Phra That Doi Suthep, the much famous and final location for our hike. Once the road leading to Doi Suthep was established in 1935, Wat Pha Lat became a residency for monks. articles.text: The de Young Museum in San Francisco is exhibiting impressionist and realist artworks from 1848 to 1960 in an exhibition entitled “American Beauty” now on display through October 20. American art in the 19th and 20th centuries presents a variety of artistic responses during a complex period in US history. The artwork featured is borrowed from the collection of Bernard and Barbro Osher. The exhibition includes the first large-scale oil painting by Winslow Homer (The Angler, ca. 1874), the first genre picture by William Merritt Chase (Spanish Bric-à-Brac Shop, 1883), the first major George Bellows landscape (In Virginia, 1908), the first Georgia O’Keeffe images of the Southwest (Front of Ranchos Church, 1930 and The Patio, 1940), as well as 13 artists whose art is being shown at the museum for the first time. To learn more about the exhibition, visit https://www.famsf. org/exhibitions/osher-american-art. The American Beauty exhibition is currently on display at de Young Museum in San Francisco.

articles.text: Vallejo-based theater company to perform The Winter’s Tale Members of Vallejo Shakespeare in the Park performing Hamlet in Dracena Park in 2023 A free performance of Shakespeare’s The Winter’s Tale will take place in Dracena Park this Sunday afternoon, August 11, at 4 p.m., presented by Vallejo Shakespeare. The performance will take place in the quarry area. Seating is first come, first served and will be picnic-style on the lawn. Audiences are encouraged to bring a blanket or a low beach chair to enjoy the performance. Friendly, well-behaved dogs are welcome but must be on a leash. Attendees are encouraged to walk, bike, or carpool to the performance, as parking in the area is limited. This performance marks the third appearance of Vallejo Shakespeare at Dracena Park. Previously, the group staged performances of Henry V in 2019 and Hamlet in 2023. Established in 2010, Vallejo Shakespeare in the Park is a live theatre group that produces one live Shakespeare production each summer, with free performances in outdoor settings across the Bay Area. The troupe uses minimal sets and costumes, instead emphasizing the individual actors’ performances. “The most amazing thing about Shakespeare is how relevant it is to this day,” said Dalia Vidor, founder of Vallejo Shakespeare in the Park. “All of Shakespeare’s plays have a very simple storyline. People unnecessarily complicate it. And I think kids can really understand them.” In addition to producing and directing the plays, Vidor also plays several roles in each production. Although she now lives in Vallejo, Vidor grew up in the Trestle Glen neighborhood and attended Crocker Highlands Elementary School in her youth where she developed a life-long love of acting. Vidor said her favorite part of each performance is getting the chance to change people’s minds about the bard’s plays. “I find it most thrilling when after the show, people come up to me or to my actors and they say how much they disliked Shakespeare because of school, [...] and how surprised they were that they enjoyed the show. Specifically, how different it was from anything they were taught,” she explained. For more information about the performance, contact the City of Piedmont at 420-3040. articles.text: The plot of The Wife is an elegant and intimate vehicle for the remarkable talent of Glenn Close as she portrays Joan Castleman, wife of Joe Castleman (impressively performed by Jonathan Pryce). For all 40 years of their marriage Joan has been content to walk in the literary shadow of Joe – college professor and accomplished novelist. However, it is at this point in their lives, the year is 1992, that the narrative hints, ever so subtly, that Joan is feeling that their relationship is becoming increasingly restrictive. The dormant emotions are triggered when Joe receives an early morning phone call at their Connecticut home, informing him that he has won the Nobel Prize in Literature. Joan is in the den, on the phone’s extension, and the camera lingers on her face as she hears this much hoped for news. Yet, briefly, the joy and excitement that she feels is eclipsed by something else, an enigmatic foreshadowing, yet to be revealed. And so, after several receptions and countless toasts and voiced congratulations, Joe and Joan and their son, David (Max Irons), leave on the Concorde for Stockholm for the Nobel awards ceremony. It is there that they step into a swirl of adulation, preparation, rehearsals and press photographs. Joe relishes and encourages the attention. What soon becomes obvious, expressed through the reactions of Joan, is that their marriage is unraveling and the honor bestowed on Joe is pushing fragile truths to the surface. Issues were once studiously buried beneath a patina of compromise and swallowed silence. Joan is growing increasingly impatient. Her signals of mounting discontent are at first discounted or simply ignored by Joe. This is his moment on the world stage. There is a something deeper at work and its import has yet to be fully revealed. The Nobel Prize is but a metaphor. Throughout the film, the camera caresses Close’s face, holds on her visage, the flash in her eyes, the set of her mouth, the tilt of her head, all silently speaking to the audience, all capturing one singular moment and then the next. It’s a master class in acting by Close, a consummate performer inhabiting a character. The Wife. Directed by Bjorn Runge. Starring Glenn Close, Jonathan Price, Christian Slater. 1 hr., 40 min. articles.text: Mark Rylance and Tom Hanks in Bridge of Spies In retrospect, the Soviet Union and the United States managed to navigate almost 50 years of adversarial encounters without a confrontation that would have taken us past the brink of the deterrence known as mutual assured destruction (aka MAD). Part of the kabuki dance that the two superpowers engaged in, however, was elaborate and the result of sustained spying. Steven Spielberg’s Bridge of Spies, is a taut and well-made film, based on a true story. It begins in 1957 with the arrest by the FBI of Soviet spy, Rudolf Abel (Mark Ryance). The government, certain it had overwhelming evidence of his clandestine activity, decided to put him on trial. James Donovan (Tom Hanks), an insurance attorney, is selected to defend Abel who has stoically resisted all attempts by the CIA to extract information from him. What the government did not anticipate was that Donovan would mount a rigorous defense on Abel’s behalf, followed by an appeal of his conviction. Donovan was denigrated for carrying out what he felt was his constitutional obligation. articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s The Wind Rises The Wind Rises was intended to be Hayao Miyazaki’s final film. It would also serve as this intensely creative animator and storyteller’s tribute to Jiro Horikoshi, known in Japan as a master aeronautical engineer and a pioneer in aircraft design during the first half of the 20th century. Through Miyazaki’s prism, Jiro (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) is portrayed as a bookish, bespectacled boy and young man (not dissimilar from Harry Potter) who possessed a dreamy, distracted manner, often lost in his imagination, his visions of airplanes filling his thoughts. Early on, Jiro so loved the idea of flight that he imagines meeting the Italian aeronautical engineer Giovanni Battista Caproni, who encourages him to pursue his love of airplanes and design. As it turns out Jiro cannot be a pilot himself because of his eyesight. And yet fly he does. As part of the story, Miyazaki includes a sad and tender romance between Jiro and a young woman, Naoko Satomi (Emily Blunt). They meet in Tokyo during Japan’s most devastating Great Kanto Earthquake in 1923, a natural disaster that all but leveled Tokyo and is grippingly captured in the film’s intense images. It is Naoko who quotes to Jiro the words of poet Paul Valéry, “The wind rises, we must try to live,” and is the source of the film’s title. In Jiro, Miyazaki creates a character of inherent idealism and innocence, qualities that thread their way through the wide spectrum of his own work. With insight and a languid beauty, using the resilient metaphor of wind, he involves, nay mesmerizes, those who gaze upon his wondrous animation, which never fails to transcend. Tweens and young teens will be enamored of Jiro and his personal quest to follow his dream. Others jaded by life and reality will recall that it was also Jiro Horikoshi who would one day design the Japanese Zero fighter aircraft used to deadly effect during WWII (Kamikaze meant “Divine Wind”). As a result, The Wind Rises opened worldwide to controversy. But it soon became Japan’s highest grossing film in 2013, was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, was awarded a Golden Globe Award for Best Foreign Language Film, and won the Japan Academy Prize for Animation of the Year. The Wind Rises, Animated from Studio Ghibli. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. With the voices of Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Emily Blunt and Martin Short. 2 hrs., 6 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2013. Now streaming on Fandango/prime/MAX

articles.text: Kodi Smit-McPhee in Alpha If you’re a parent of a tween or a newbie teen who may be feeling a bit anxious about the approaching first day of school, we suggest seeing the movie Alpha. It’s a wonderful merging of old-fashioned story-telling and state-ofthe art technology, creating a solidly engaging and riveting tale about a boy who out of kindness and then necessity befriends an injured wolf. But this narrative is not of the Lassie Come Home genre. The film is set in southwestern Europe, just as the Ice Age is coming to a close, meaning some 20,000 years ago. The story opens with Tau (Johannes Haukur Johannesson), the clan’s chief, leading a small cohort of hunters, to include his teenage son, Keda (Kodi Smit McPhee), on a bison hunt. Actually the strategy is to charge at the animals, herd them toward a cliff where some will drop to their deaths and can then be butchered and skinned later. During the stampede, Keda is thrown off the same cliff by a massive bison, falling onto a ledge some 20 feet below, knocked unconscious. His father is frantic but realizes that reaching his son is impossible and will risk his own death. Sadly, he is uncertain if Keda is still alive. Painfully, grief-stricken, the hunters leave Keda, stopping only to salvage the hides and meat of the bison deep in the gorge, and then start for home. And so begins the boy’s journey of survival. He is injured, his right ankle severely damaged from the fall. And he must find a way off the ledge. Remarkably, it begins to rain in torrents, and the deep canyon below is filled with flash flooding water. Having no choice, Keda drops down into the muddy waters, waking up on a muddy bank, the waters having receded. Placing his ankle between two rocks he snaps it back into place, fashions a splint with sticks and leather thongs, and slowly, awkwardly, limps toward the horizon. Soon he hears the howl of wolves. Terrified, he finds a gnarled and desiccated tree, and. with the wolves close behind, he clings to a wide branch as the wolves circle below. As the sun sets, Keda sees that one of the wolves has been injured and realizes that the wolf pack has left, leaving the wounded wolf below. His mother, Nu (Mercedes de Zerda), had counseled that Tau “leads with his heart, not his spear.” And so, at sunrise, Keda climbs down and begins to care for the wolf. And thus begins the story of a boy and a wolf and the start of a long, forced march toward the home of his clan. It is a precarious and perilous “walk about,” requiring that Keda and the wolf, eventually named Alpha, gradually learn to trust, then protect one another, as well as hunt as a team. As their journey continues, they are tested by predators and the elements. Alpha is gorgeous to look at, the landscapes breathtaking, the vastness of a deep blue sky, the distant horizons stunning. At night, in the heavens, the stars are a blanket of white and swirling pink. It is from that map of stars, marked on Keda’s hand by his father, which helps him find true north and the path leading home. As well, embedded in Alpha are countless questions about what life must have been like for a boy some 20,000 years ago. This is a classic, straightforward adventure film, as well as a rite of passage moment in Keda’s life. It’s compelling and thrilling, and a great end-of-summer movie. One tangential point: this story can be intense and has its harrowing moments. It may be more than some youngsters can handle. Alpha. Directed by Albert Hughes. Starring Kodi Smith, Jens Hulténm Natasha Malthe. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2018. Streaming on prime/Fandango/apple tv.

articles.text: Benji (2018) is a remake of the popular 1974 family-friendly film that focuses on the love of a stray dog by two latchkey kids, Carter and Frankie Hughes (Gabriel Bateman and Darby Camp) who recently lost their father, and live with their single mom, Whitney Hughes (Kiele Sanchez). The story opens when a mother canine and her small litter are taken to the animal shelter by a malevolent dogcatcher. Out of the shadows appears the face of a pint-sized pooch, watching as the family is carted off. He is a mixed-breed dog who lives on the street, searching for food wherever he can find it. In his travels, he meets up with Carter and Frankie. They try and feed him some strawberries, but he is cautious and timid; however, he quickly realizes that the kids will not hurt him and follows them home. Carter spots the little guy outside, and they decide to bring him inside. Uncertain of their mom’s reaction they hide him under a pile of stuffed animals. Frankie wants to name him after Benjamin Franklin, which naturally gets shortened to Benji. When mom discovers Benji, she insists that the kids take the stray back where they found him. With regret they obey, and leaving Benji to fend for himself they stop off at Mr. Sam’s Pawn Shop (Gralen Bryant Banks). Without their knowing, Benji follows them. To their surprise, they walk into the middle of a robbery carried out by two thugs (Will Rothhaar and Angus Sampson). When one of their masks slips off, they realize that Carter and Frankie can identify them and so they kidnap the kids, forcing them into a van. Benji, who has been outside waiting, sees this taking place and chases after the van, all the way to the robbers’ hideout, a large, decaying plantation house. Watching the kids being taken into the house, and seeing that the men own a mean-looking Rottweiler, Benji hurries back to Grant and Frankie’s home where he tries to convince Whitney and a friendly cop, Lyle (Jerod Haynes), to follow him back to the hideout. Of course the children in the audience are rooting for Benji, and hoping that the adults will figure out what Benji is trying to say. But since Benji never utters a word, the filmmakers never using voice over or CGI lip movement. All that Benji urgently wants to say must be conveyed by his facial expressions. Of course, there are harrowing moments, chases, and the challenge to outwit the bad guys in order to rescue the kids. The children in the audience will be riveted to the story, and definitely will fall in love with Benji. Benji. Written and Directed by Brandon Camp. Starring Gabriel Bateman, Darby Camp, Kiele Sanchez. 1 hr., 27 min. Rated G. Released 2018, Now streaming on Netflix A scene from the 2018 remake of Benji

articles.text: Bonita Avenue School was Piedmont’s first public school, built in 1909 and designed by Albert Farr. The first order of business was to build a city hall and a school. While the Board of Trustees debated the location of City Hall (some wanted it on Highland Avenue), plans progressed for Piedmont’s first public school. The Bonita Avenue School was built in 1909. It had eight classrooms for eight teachers who taught eight grades and 318 students. The Lake School (now the Egbert W. Beach School) on Lake Avenue) was built three years later to provide more classrooms for students. The first school was built on the east side of Bonita Avenue between Oakland and Vista Avenues, hence the name, Bonita Avenue School. When Frank C. Havens died in 1918, the school was renamed in his memory. Albert Farr designed the school in the Spanish Colonial or Spanish Mission design that he would use the following year for Piedmont’s City Hall and the Oakland Avenue Bridge. The school had two large, square Spanish towers with shallow balconies and ornate cupolas on each side of the main building. Classroom wings on each side extended to the front and rear, making the building an H-shape with the school’s entry set between the two wings. Large arched windows flanked the arched entry, and Mission tile covered the roofs and capped the walls to the courtyard entry. Clara Crumpton was the first principal of the Bonita Avenue School and taught first grade. On the occasion of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco in 1915, Miss Crumpton had her students recreate the “Tower of Jewels” in front of the school. In 1910 Ellen Driscoll began teaching at the school, and became principal of Havens School from 1920 to 1940. She was a popular teacher and was known for her keen memory as a principal. She knew the names of each of her 300 students. The 1947 photo shows the school with its courtyard and classroom wings. The long, rectangular building at the rear is a 5-classroom addition completed in 1937 by the Federal government as a Work Projects Administration project. In 1940 the Board of Education contracted again with the WPA to build auditoriums for what by then were three elementary schools. The auditorium at Havens was dedicated as the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse. An aerial photo in 1947 shows the original Bonita Avenue School with the 1938 classroom addition across the back, and the auditorium added in 1940.

articles.text: The April 18, 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire sent thousands of San Franciscans fleeing to the East Bay. The fires and smoke were visible for days from the Piedmont hills as over 15,000 lost their homes in the fire. While there were no reports of refugees camping in Piedmont Park, some refugees did stay with friends in Piedmont. As Oakland looked to the hills to annex more land for this influx of earthquake survivors, a group of far-sighted Piedmont residents did not want Piedmont to become part of Oakland. Hugh Craig and James Ballentine immediately began an effort to incorporate Piedmont as a city. They quickly drew up a map of Piedmont’s borders using an existing Piedmont Sanitary District map and filed the map in Sacramento. On January 26, 1907, Piedmonters voted to incorporate. The vote passed, and Piedmont officially became a municipality four days later, January 30, 1907. A photo from 1926 shows Ellen Driscoll, then the principal of Havens School, with her students. Under the guidance of Clara Crumpton, the first principal of the Bonita Avenue School, students recreated the Tower of Jewels, the centerpiece of the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco.

Clara Crumpton was the first principal of the Bonita Avenue School and taught first grade. On the occasion of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco in 1915, Miss Crumpton had her students recreate the “Tower of Jewels” in front of the school. In 1910 Ellen Driscoll began teaching at the school, and became principal of Havens School from 1920 to 1940. She was a popular teacher and was known for her keen memory as a principal. She knew the names of each of her 300 students. The 1947 photo shows the school with its courtyard and classroom wings. The long, rectangular building at the rear is a 5-classroom addition completed in 1937 by the Federal government as a Work Projects Administration project. In 1940 the Board of Education contracted again with the WPA to build auditoriums for what by then were three elementary schools. The auditorium at Havens was dedicated as the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse. Hand-painted panels in the ceiling of all three school auditoriums were executed by 5th and 6th grade students in a paintby-number fashion. At the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse, they depict California history. In 1953, the Piedmont Board of Education considered the 1909 Havens School to be inadequate to meet the school enrollment at the time. The number of students had grown to the point where some classrooms were in temporary buildings. A bond issue was passed, and the new Frank C. Havens School, designed by nationally recognized architects Miller-Warnecke, was completed in 1955 with 12 classrooms, a library, an administration office and cafeteria. At Witter they found workers were applying the top, burnt orange surface over a recently laid, black undersurface. In 1898 Piedmont real estate developer Frank C. Havens developed the Piedmont Springs Park attraction. It had a grand, palm-lined entrance that later became Palm Drive. One of the first improvements Havens made was the creation of a living hedge maze modeled after Hampton Court in England. The Maze was demolished when a new School Board purchased part of the park land in 1920 for its new high school and athletic field. The Maze was where Witter Field is today. The City also purchased Havens’ remaining park land for the current Piedmont Park. The original Witter Field surface was grass and the track around it was less than a quarter mile. The field was re-dedicated as the Witter Sports Complex in 1998 with a new synthetic turf field, a full quarter mile track, new baseball and softball fields, and a new field house. Witter Field’s original synthetic turf and track were replaced in 2007 because they were worn out. By the mid- 2010s they needed to be replaced again. Witter’s underground drainage system also needed to be replaced, as rain regularly flooded the field. The renovation was expected to be paid for with Measure H1 bond funds that Piedmont voters approved in 2016 for new high school facilities. However, construction costs exceeded estimates and the work at Witter was postponed. In February 2019, it was announced the project, which had been tentatively scheduled for that spring and summer, was being delayed for at least another year. The contractor discovered 60,000 square feet of substandard asphalt base needed to be removed and replaced before the track could be paved. articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Apricot and Almond Tea Cake is a sure-fire favorite for any occasion. This is a bonafide pantry cake! The opportunity for swaps is abundant in this simple cake, depending on what is available when the mood strikes to bake. Any variety of dried fruit should work, cherries, cranberries, dates, etc. Rehydrate accordingly to ensure a tender texture in the cake. If the dried fruit is soft and pliable, then skip the rehydration step. Either almond extract or vanilla extract will be delicious. If you don’t have either, try taking the melted butter to the next level and brown it slightly to impart its slightly nutty taste to the cake. The topping may be made with any nuts – finely chopped walnuts or pecans would be delicious. Or make a quick streusel, with or without nuts. Apricot and Almond Tea Cake Adapted from Food 52/Sarah Jampel Makes a shallow 10-inch cake INGREDIENTS • 1⁄2 cup unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly • 1⁄4 cup sour cream • 1 cup granulated sugar, divided 7⁄8 cup for the cake and 1⁄8 cup for the top of the cake • 2 eggs • 11⁄2 cup all-purpose flour • 1⁄2 teaspoon baking soda • 1⁄8 teaspoon salt • 1⁄3 cup dried apricots, diced into 1⁄4-inch pieces • 1 teaspoon fresh lemon zest • 1⁄2 teaspoon almond extract (substitute 1 teaspoon vanilla extract) • 3⁄4 cup sliced almonds INSTRUCTIONS 1. Position an oven rack in the middle position, and preheat oven to 350° F. Generously butter the bottom and sides of a 10-inch pie plate. 2. Rehydrate the diced apricots in a small bowl and cover with warm water. Let sit for 5-10 minutes, then drain the water and spread out on a clean towel to dry the pieces on all sides. You want to get them as dry as possible. This step is optional if your dried fruit is soft and pliable. 3. Combine the flour, baking soda salt in a small bowl. Whisk gently to blend thoroughly. 4. Combine the melted butter, sour cream and 7⁄8’s cup of sugar in a large bowl and mix well to combine. (Can be done either by hand with a sturdy whisk or a hand mixer.) 5. Add the eggs, one at a time, mixing well after each addition. Add the almond extract and lemon zest. 6. Add the flour mixture and mix gently until well incorporated but taking care to avoid over-mixing. Fold in the dried apricots. 7. Pour the batter into the prepared pie plate and smooth to level the surface. Sprinkle the sliced almonds atop in an even layer; then sprinkle on the remaining 1⁄8 cup of granulated sugar in a thin, even layer on top of the sliced almonds. 8. Bake for 30-35 minutes until a toothpick inserted into the center of the cake comes out clean, and the cake and almonds are golden brown. 9. Cool completely before slicing. (The most difficult part of this recipe!) 10. Sit back and smile at what you have created.

articles.text: Casimir “Kaz” Lawler of Piedmont passed away peacefully on Sunday, July 14th after a short battle with cancer. He had lived in the same house in Piedmont for 57 years. At 89, Kaz lived a full life. Born to Michael and Bertha Lawler, Kaz was raised in the Manayunk area of Philadelphia, PA and attended Villanova University where he studied Civil Engineering and was a part of the Navy ROTC program. During his commute to college Kaz met his future wife, Gloria. After graduation Kaz attended flight school with the US Navy and was assigned to be a transport pilot, moving men and materials around the world. In order to make it to his wedding, Kaz secured a special 24-hour pass to fly from Pensacola, Florida to Philadelphia, PA. Kaz later qualified to fly on aircraft carriers and served during the Cuban Missile Crisis on the USS Essex, the first US carrier to enforce the quarantine. During the Vietnam War Kaz flew the largest carrier plane, the A3 Skywarrior, from the smallest carrier, the USS Hancock, making over 150 carrier landings. From the USS Hancock, Kaz flew missions to refuel fighter jets in the air over the Gulf of Tonkin, as well as electronic counter-measure combat missions to protect the planes in flight and ships at sea. With the Navy, Kaz and Gloria moved many places around the country and raised a family of five children. They settled in Piedmont in 1967 when Kaz was assigned to the USS Hancock. In 1970, Kaz retired from Casimir “Kaz” Lawler of Piedmont died on July 14, 2024. He was 89. active duty to spend more time with his family. He worked as an engineer for the Naval Air Rework Facility in Alameda and retired as head of Quality Control for the Navy’s S3 Viking and the A3 Skywarrior aircraft. Kaz enjoyed traveling with Gloria throughout the world, visiting 35 countries. Kaz also loved traveling with the entire extended family, especially to Paris. Kaz is preceded in death by his beloved wife Gloria. He is survived by five children, nine grandchildren and one great-grandchild. He is additionally survived by a sister and brother. articles.text: In the midst of summer heat, it’s hard to think about the cool fall days ahead. For your garden, now is the ideal time to start sowing seeds for the next growing season. Fall gardening is one of the most underrated seasons; there are less weeds, fewer pests, and often more rain to help out with watering. Here are a few key takeaways to consider before planting for cool season harvests. As soon as your spring and summer crops stop producing, pull them to make room for all those delicious fall and winter crops. Start cool season vegetables in their place while we still have long days and warm soil. By the time brisk weather arrives, your plants will be strong, sturdy, and well established for whatever fall throws their way. Clean up garden beds by hoeing weeds, adding lots of compost, broadforking the soil to allow for air and moisture infiltration, and topping with mulch. Mulching in summer is key to moderating soil temperatures and keeping all that irrigation moisture in the ground. Watering is the most important task for your newly planted fall garden. High temperatures and low humidity mean that you’ll need to check the moisture of your seedlings often while they establish. If the heat of the sun is too intense, consider adding a lightweight shade cloth over your garden bed to keep things cool. Rita’s harvest of fall carrots Fall can really feel like a second spring. Here’s a selection of a few vegetables to plant in late summer to keep your garden growing through autumn. Broccoli and kale mature well in cool weather and will not be bothered by the cabbage moth as they are in spring weather. Root crops, like carrots and beets, will take longer but are worth the wait since they grow sweeter as the days get cooler. Snap and snow peas start producing in 60 days, and peas that mature in cold weather seem especially sweet and crisp. The real stars of the fall garden are Asian greens, like tatsoi, pak choi, mizuna, and napa cabbage. Quick-maturing varieties can even be harvested in 45 days. We are so lucky to be California gardeners with a long growing season. So, freshen up your empty beds with some compost and get ready to plant your second garden. He persuaded a reluctant General Dwight Eisenhower to support the French Resistance and FreeFrance with troops and tanks. To reach his starting point at Montparnasse station, LeClerc fought off heavily armed enemy troops surrounding Paris. A Secret Command Center Liberation Museum sits atop a historical secret bunker. It is a featured exhibit, built as a command center meant to protect against air strikes. If under attack, the essential public services of Paris could be powered from this location. The government could manage vital communication systems that control water, electricity, telephone, and hospitals. The bunker’s private telephone exchange was independent of public access and equipped with 250 telephone numbers. It had its own air supply and capacity for recirculating air like a submarine. Its 1930s diesel-powered generator kept the lights on, and as a backup, a bicycle-built-for-two was converted for pedal-power. During the war, the Germans knew the bunker location with identity as an air raid shelter. They had no knowledge of its command-center features. It was a fear-obsessed era when the public grew panicky about poison-gas attacks. It was commonly known that poison-gas canisters of mustard-gas were in abundant supply, left-over from World War I. The populace knew that poison-gas injuries were severe and terrifying, and they feared imminent air-attacks of poison gas – attacks that never came. The command bunker’s fate was to sit idly in neglect for years. But the French Resistance discovered its value for clandestine activities such as a hideout, or trading post for messengers. Most significantly, Resistance Exodus of the French fleeing before the German troops arrive. More than eight million French were displaced or fled the Nazi occupation during WWII leaders used the command center to organize the Parisian military strike against the German occupiers. The start of World War II World War II started in Europe when Germany bombed Poland’s Danzig naval port, followed by a ground invasion on September 1, 1939. The Polish Army fought back hard, but the battle was lost when Russia invaded from the east. Joseph Stalin had signed a pact with Adolph Hitler for a surprise attack. Russia wanted the territory it lost at the Versailles Treaty after World War I. In a north-south boundary agreement, Germany took western Poland and Russia got the eastern half. Europe was frantic over the Polish invasion. France declared war on Germany and then waited and watched for the first strike during the next eight months. France’s war declaration devolved into ridicule with jokes about “the phony war.” Then, abruptly, German armies broke into a blitzkrieg, overrunning Belgium and the Netherlands, driving the British into the sea at Dunkirk; and defeating France. Upon defeat, Parisians gathered sadly to watch a stream of Reich motorcades speeding victoriously into the heart of the city. The City of Light had surrendered to avoid destruction. Paris would be flooded with German Army troops. The Supreme commandants selected the finest hotels, Le Meurice, Le Ritz, Lutetia, George V, Le Crillon – to set up shop. The Fuhrer’s objective was to neutralize France militarily, contain and source Paris with its industry-rich environs, and control the seaports. Calais, just 21 miles across the English Channel, was situated favorably for a ground strike against England. The North Atlantic coastline ports – Brest, Saint-Nazaire, and Bordeaux – were brought to heel. the Reich blocked vital war shipments to the Allies, especially from the United States. France suffers Allied Bombings Few Americans are familiar with the Western Allied bombings of civilian installations in German-occupied France during WWII. The Germans’ use of France’s coastline ports as bases for their U-boats made the cities an unintentional target where the Allies were forced to deliberate about the loss of civilian lives in their ongoing recalculations of essential military strategies to weaken the Germans. Collateral damage in terms of human lives during wartime is an uncomfortable debate and an unconscionable reality, but the museum exhibits do not shy away from the killings that caused severe hostilities between nations on the same side of the war. The Paris-La Chapelle marshalling yard is a critical example of an Anglo-U.S. bombing raid that killed 670 workers propagandized by the Germans to taunt the French about their very own military-partners attacking French countrymen. The French are schooled and can ably recite war legends of their country’s devastating loss to Germany followed by the Paris occupation during four agonizing years. They rise to a high note at the German expulsion on August 25, 1944, France’s Liberation Day. Le Musée de la Liberation de Paris on the Left Bank just south of Montparnasse was opened in 2019 – exactly 75 years to the day that Paris drove the Nazis out of the city. The museum’s intriguing mix of film, soundtrack, photography and artifacts create the Paris story from defeat and humiliation to liberation. A serious and somber experience, the visitor travels back to learn firsthand the fear and harsh realities inside an occupied city in a brutal war. From its depths, one is delivered to victory with a huge sigh of relief. The museum’s presentation is an intricate weave of the victors: the French Resistance and Free-France forces that mustered to fight and defeat the Germans in Paris. The week-long battle was hard-fought. The German retreat signaled a turning point in France’s liberation and the end of the war. The United States proudly enjoined in the French attack, and they shared the Paris victory. The full name of the Liberation Museum is Le Musée de la Libération de Paris - le Musée du Général LeClerc – Musée Jean Moulin to denote three collections of related artifacts now wrapped into one museum. Though its name is unnecessarily lengthy, it serves to spotlight two celebrated war heroes, General LeClerc of Free-France and Jean Moulin, the renowned chief architect of the French Resistance. LeClerc is a pseudonym he adopted in the interest of protecting family The Liberation Museum of Paris during his far-reaching military career. LeClerc’s role was significant, leading Free-France forces. He persuaded a reluctant General Dwight Eisenhower to support the French Resistance and FreeFrance with troops and tanks. To reach his starting point at Montparnasse station, LeClerc fought off heavily armed enemy troops surrounding Paris. A Secret Command Center Liberation Museum sits atop a historical secret bunker. It is a featured exhibit, built as a command center meant to protect against air strikes. If under attack, the essential public services of Paris could be powered from this location. The government could manage vital communication systems that control water, electricity, telephone, and hospitals. The bunker’s private telephone exchange was independent of public access and equipped with 250 telephone numbers. It had its own air supply and capacity for recirculating air like a submarine. Its 1930s diesel-powered generator kept the lights on, and as a backup, a bicycle-built-for-two was converted for pedal-power. During the war, the Germans knew the bunker location with identity as an air raid shelter. They had no knowledge of its command-center features. It was a fear-obsessed era when the public grew panicky about poison-gas attacks. It was commonly known that poison-gas canisters of mustard-gas were in abundant supply, left-over from World War I. The populace knew that poison-gas injuries were severe and terrifying, and they feared imminent air-attacks of poison gas – attacks that never came. The command bunker’s fate was to sit idly in neglect for years. But the French Resistance discovered its value for clandestine activities such as a hideout, or trading post for messengers. Most significantly, Resistance Exodus of the French fleeing before the German troops arrive. More than eight million French were displaced or fled the Nazi occupation during WWII leaders used the command center to organize the Parisian military strike against the German occupiers. The start of World War II World War II started in Europe when Germany bombed Poland’s Danzig naval port, followed by a ground invasion on September 1, 1939. The Polish Army fought back hard, but the battle was lost when Russia invaded from the east. Joseph Stalin had signed a pact with Adolph Hitler for a surprise attack. Russia wanted the territory it lost at the Versailles Treaty after World War I. In a north-south boundary agreement, Germany took western Poland and Russia got the eastern half. Europe was frantic over the Polish invasion. France declared war on Germany and then waited and watched for the first strike during the next eight months. France’s war declaration devolved into ridicule with jokes about “the phony war.” Then, abruptly, German armies broke into a blitzkrieg, overrunning Belgium and the Netherlands, driving the British into the sea at Dunkirk; and defeating France. Upon defeat, Parisians gathered sadly to watch a stream of Reich motorcades speeding victoriously into the heart of the city. The City of Light had surrendered to avoid destruction. Paris would be flooded with German Army troops. The Supreme commandants selected the finest hotels, Le Meurice, Le Ritz, Lutetia, George V, Le Crillon – to set up shop. The Fuhrer’s objective was to neutralize France militarily, contain and source Paris with its industry-rich environs, and control the seaports. Calais, just 21 miles across the English Channel, was situated favorably for a ground strike against England. The North Atlantic coastline ports – Brest, Saint-Nazaire, and Bordeaux – were brought to heel. By controlling the waterways, the Reich blocked vital war shipments to the Allies, especially from the United States. unaccounted numbers of materiel and resources to supply the Axis power’s aggression against France’s own interests. In truth, the Americans allied with Great Britain flew hundreds of bombing raids against French cities under German-control, killing 68,778 civilians – men, women, and children – during WWII. Possibly there was no darker time in modern France. France suffers Allied Bombings Few Americans are familiar with the Western Allied bombings of civilian installations in German-occupied France during WWII. The Germans’ use of France’s coastline ports as bases for their U-boats made the cities an unintentional target where the Allies were forced to deliberate about the loss of civilian lives in their ongoing recalculations of essential military strategies to weaken the Germans. Collateral damage in terms of human lives during wartime is an uncomfortable debate and an unconscionable reality, but the museum exhibits do not shy away from the killings that caused severe hostilities between nations on the same side of the war. The Paris-La Chapelle marshalling yard is a critical example of an Anglo-U.S. bombing raid that killed 670 workers propagandized by the Germans to taunt the French about their very own military-partners attacking French countrymen. The temple is a serene location in the middle of the bamboo forest; with ancient architecture to awe at. There is a Naga Staircase, two mythical serpent creatures down a stairwell. In Buddhist religion, the Nagas are known as protectors of the temple to ward off evil spirits. There are also three Chedis on the Wat Pha Lat grounds, which are large sacred structures that are known to house precious relics from Buddha or revered monks. There’s also a Viharn to worship Buddha. Stepping inside the building requires patrons to remove their shoes, like all temples in Thailand. Although I spotted many people in shorts, it’s not recommended to wear shorts or cutoff clothing on holy grounds in order to pay respect to Buddha. It’d be wise to keep light pants in your pack. The hike to Wat Pha Lat is a popular one, passing 46 hikers in the 0.8 mile span to the monastery before passing an uncountable amount of people walking around the temple grounds. Wat Pha Lat has a parking lot for those disinterested in putting on their hiking boots, while there are also taxis available for those wanting a short-cut to the renowned Wat Phra That Doi Suthep up the road. Venturing from Wat Pha Lat to Wat Phra That Doi Suthep by foot turns a moderate hike into a difficult one; it should only be traversed by skilled hikers ready to get their hands dirty. Although it adds just 1.4 miles of hiking to your day, you’ll pick up nearly 1,500 feet in elevation gain, requiring hikers to bring their knees all the way to your chest on some steep sections. Marching in humidity around 80 percent caused this Bay Area born-and-raised hiker to look like he jumped out of a pool when reaching Doi Suthep. But the path to Doi Suthep is extraordinary and cuts you away from the bounds of foot traffic on the Monk’s Trail to Wat Pha Lat. After hiking up the remainder of the Monk’s Trail, you’ll intersect with Sriwichai Alley (route 1004), walking left to take the Pilgrim’s Path on the opposite side of the road. Created in 1383, Wat Phra That Doi Suthep is named after the mountain which it is located and considered to be the most sacred temple in all of Thailand. There’s another magnificent Naga Staircase leading to the temple, this one much larger and colorful than the previous at Wat Pha Lat. Peer closely at the scales of the two serpents leading you towards Doi Suthep. Entrance to the monastery costs ฿100, which is just $2.85— it is also recommended to dress appropriately, so no tank tops. Some monasteries do not allow people wearing shorts as well, but if you’re traveling in July or August, some make exceptions like at Doi Suthep. You’ll find sweeping views of Chiang Mai from multiple overlooks on the grounds and several large statues of Buddha. You’ll also be required to take your shoes off when entering the primary section of the temple, where there’s a spectacular large golden Chedi, which towers 79 feet in height. Should hikers call it a day, you’ll end your hike at around 2.5 miles with over 2,000 feet in elevation gain. Taxis will be ready at the base of Doi Suthep to take your group back into town. Heading back down the road and onto the trails makes it a 4.5 mile day of hiking. Keep in mind some steep sections coupled with usual wet conditions in Thailand could make things difficult for a descent. Hikers should wear proper footgear for tackling the Monk’s Trail and Pilgrim’s Trail, along with packing mosquito repellent to keep away the pesky critters. The intent of this mural is to showcase plant and animal ecosystems native to JMP. The images include snakes, bees, fox, deer, quail, scrub jay, redwoods, blackberries, star tulip, and California poppies. The murals were truly a team effort over a year in the making and FoJMP is so grateful to the donors and artists who made them possible for park-goers to enjoy for years to come.
